claims.text: In-situ formation of finely dispersed nanoscale Y2O3 precipitates is the key mechanism governing high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural alloys.
Nanoscale Y2O3 precipitates impede dislocation glide.
Nanoscale Y2O3 precipitates reduce grain-boundary sliding.
Impeded dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding promote work hardening and energy dissipation during high-temperature deformation.
Controlled addition of a small amount of yttria followed by thermal or chemical treatment will induce in-situ precipitation of nanoscale Y2O3 particles.
The 800–1200 K range is relevant to fusion plasma-facing component deformation.
The in-situ Y2O3 particles are stable microstructural pinning centers.
Y2O3-mediated pinning retards strain localization and dynamic recovery.
Y2O3-mediated dislocation pinning increases the work-hardening rate and stabilizes the microstructure against high-temperature softening.
Relative to an untreated baseline, the yttria-treated alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to an untreated baseline, the yttria-treated alloy will have a higher work-hardening rate.
Relative to an untreated baseline, the yttria-treated alloy will have improved high-temperature fracture toughness because strain localization is reduced.
Without nanoscale oxide precipitates, the baseline material softens more rapidly at high temperature because dislocation glide and grain-boundary sliding are unimpeded.
The proposed effect is limited to 800–1200 K and to yttria additions that retain a nanoscale dispersion rather than forming coarse oxides.
Irradiation and long-term thermal exposure may modulate the strength and toughness effects.
The proposed controlled comparison uses yttria-treated and untreated samples with otherwise identical preparation and tests them at 800–1200 K.
TEM will be used to verify precipitate presence, size, and distribution while mechanical tests measure yield strength, work-hardening rate, and fracture toughness.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if the treated alloy lacks a statistically significant increase in the three predicted properties or if meaningful nanoscale oxide precipitation is not observed.
